[MUQATIL:64:5-6/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Their messengers brought clear explanations, but the people objected that humans would guide them and so disbelieved and turned away.
[MUQATIL:64:5-6/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God has no need of His creatures' worship and is rich beyond them.
[MUQATIL:64:5-6/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God is praised in His dominion by His creatures.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Afaʿala commonly makes an intransitive verb causative: dakhala, kharaja, and jalasa become adkhalahu, akhrajahu, and ajlasahu when another agent causes the action.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs use aftantu, aḥzantu, arjaʿtu, and aʿwartu ʿaynahu to mean making someone or something acquire that state.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Several verbs allow paired intransitive and transitive forms for putting a state into something, including jabara/jabartuhu and rakaḍat/rakaḍtu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The faʿalt causative meaning to make someone become something is rare; examples are faṭartuhu fa-afṭara and bashartuhu fa-abshara.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Khaṭṭaʾtuhu means called him a wrongdoer, like calling someone fāsiq or zānī; ḥayyaytuhu is a greeting, while saqaytuhu and raʿaytuhu can express a prayer for him.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Asqaytuhu is also used in the sense of saqaytuhu; Dhū al-Rumma's poem about watering the ruins illustrates this usage.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Afaʿaltuhu can expose someone to an event, as in aqtaltuhu, exposed him to killing; qabartuhu means buried him, while aqbartuhu provided him a grave.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Saqaytuhu means he drank what I gave; asqaytuhu means I provided water and a supply, paralleling kasawtuhu/albastuhu; shafaytuhu cures, while ashfaytuhu gives a cure.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Afaʿala can mean acquiring a condition: ajraba, anḥaza, and aḥāla mean becoming affected by mange, wasting, or livestock loss; related forms describe a person who owns such traits or resources.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Alāma r-rajulu means he became deserving of blame, whereas lāmahu means he reproached him; similar forms describe having abundant or scarce means.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Aṣrama, amḍagha, aḥṣada, and ajazza describe crops that have become ready to be cut, chewed, or harvested; the simple verb reports actually doing the act.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Faʿala and afaʿala can sometimes share causative meaning, as in fariḥa/farriḥahu or afraḥahu, gharima/gharramahu or aghramahu, and similar pairs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ḥamidtu means I rewarded him and gave his due, whereas aḥmadtu means I found him deserving of praise, like crops becoming ready for cutting.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Arāba means becoming a person of suspicion, while rābanī means causing suspicion in me; the distinction parallels becoming worthy of blame versus reproaching someone.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Khalīl says some faʿalt/afʿalt pairs have the same meaning but differ by dialect, such as qalaltu/alqaltu, šaġaltu/ašġaltu, and bakartu/abkartu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh gives further synonymous dialect forms, including qalaltu/alqaltu, šaġaltu/ašġaltu, ṣarra/aṣarra, and bakara/abkara.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Aṣbaḥnā, amsaynā, asḥarnā, and afjarnā mean entering those times of day; ṣabbaḥnā and similar simple forms mean visiting someone then.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbs such as yušajjaʿu, yujabbanu, and yuqawwā describe someone being labeled or charged with those qualities; šanuʿa can similarly be said of a person.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ghallaqa can describe repeated work closing many doors; aghlaqa is also good for plural doors, and al-Farazdaq's verse attests aghliqu abwāban.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr distinguished nazaltu from anzaltu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abāna and istabāna can be used with or without the added object form to mean that a thing became clear or that one made it clear, with paired forms sharing meaning.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The forms ṭaradtu and aṭradtu differ: the first means I drove him away, while the second means I made him a fugitive; hounds ṭaradna the game by driving it along.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ṭalaʿa means appeared, aṭlaʿa ʿalayhim means came upon them, šariqa means appeared, and ašraqa means shone; asraʿa means hastened and abṭaʾa means delayed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Saraʿa and baṭuʾa describe inherent qualities like lightness and heaviness and are not transitive, unlike ṭawwaltu l-amr or ʿajjalته.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Khalīl says fatanahu and ḥazanahu mean putting temptation or grief into someone, like kaḥaltuhu and dahantuhu; making someone tempting or sad instead takes aftanahu or aḥzanahu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Shatara r-rajulu and shatarat ʿaynuhu are distinct formations; to make a man squint, use aštarahu, just as afzaʿahu differs from faziʿa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | One group transmits Nuṣayb's poetic line with sawadtu, as in sawadtu fa-lam amlik sawādī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابافتراقفعلتوأفعلتفيالفعلللمعنى)#682/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Another group reads the line as suddat, interpreting it as a faʿalt form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماجاءفعلمنهعلىغيرفعلته)#685/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as majnūn, maslūl, and mazqūm derive from underlying verbs like janantuhu or salaltuhu even when those verbs are unused; replacement verbs can make the unused forms unnecessary.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماجاءفعلمنهعلىغيرفعلته)#685/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Janna and salla can mean putting madness or illness into someone, like ḥazuna and raḏula; janantuhu means I put madness in you, parallel to aqbartuhu giving someone a grave.
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A fronted or postponed locative does not raise the noun: the noun remains a nominative subject, while the locative supplies its setting, as in fīhā ʿAbd Allāh.
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A locative before the subject can form a complete sentence, and an inna construction allows it to be shifted after the noun without changing its role.
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the locative precedes a nominative predicate it may be ungoverning; with an accusative predicate it separates subject from predicate, and the subject licenses the circumstantial accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A locative can mark where a state holds while the predicate remains built on its subject, as in huwa laka khāliṣ or ʿAbd Allāh qāʾim fīhā.
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | The phrase khāliṣa yawma l-qiyāma is read with khāliṣa nominative or accusative; the accusative is more common because it functions like a verbal noun, khulūṣan. | mentions 7:32
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Predicates can precede a locative and be accusative as circumstantial modifiers; rajul ṣidq maʿlūman describes a fact in that state, while nominative can make the word adjectival.
[SIBAWAYH:لأنهخبرلمعروفيرتفععلىالابتداءقدمتهأوأخرته|وذلكقولكفيها#241/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Khalīl analyzes ḥasana ummuhu karīman abūhā as describing a quality established for the mother in that circumstance; nominative is also possible as an adjective.
[AKHFASH:v2p543#2/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The plural verb yahdūnanā agrees with bashar because the word has a collective sense.
[TAB-FULL:v23p8#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Earlier peoples were punished because messengers brought clear proofs establishing their call’s truth, but the people arrogantly rejected human messengers and the truth brought by their peers.
[TAB-FULL:v23p8#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Their question rejects the idea that human beings like themselves could guide them, expressing disdain

for following truth from their own kind.
[TAB-FULL:v23p8#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verb is plural because bashar, singular in form, carries a collective meaning; hence “they guide us,” not “he guides us.”
[TAB-FULL:v23p8#3/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | They disbelieved and turned away from truth; God needed none of them, for He is independent of all creation.
[TAB-FULL:v23p8#3/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | God has no need of them or their faith in Him and His messengers, and needs nothing from them.
[TAB-FULL:v23p8#3/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | God is independent of all creation and praised by all for His favors and generous acts toward them.
[TAB-FULL:v23p8/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Addressing Quraysh’s polytheists, al-Ṭabarī recalls earlier disbelieving peoples, including Noah’s, ʿĀd, Thamūd, Abraham’s, and Lot’s communities. | mentions 64:5
[NAHHAS:v4p441/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The pronoun hāʾ refers to the account, and what follows explains it as the predicate of anna.
[NAHHAS:v4p441/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs and arguments.
[NAHHAS:v4p441/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Yahdūnanā follows the plural sense of bashar, while yahdīnā would follow its singular form.
[NAHHAS:v4p441/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · المازني | reports | Al-Mazini says three nafar or raht is allowed because these denote a small group, while qawm and bashar span larger or all numbers and do not work in that construction.
[NAHHAS:v4p441/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · محمد بن يزيد | reports | Muhammad ibn Yazid disagrees with al-Mazini's explanation for bashar, noting that bashar can be singular or plural, as in 12:31, while agreeing on the other cases. | mentions 12:31
[NAHHAS:v4p441/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | They denied God's prophets and signs, turned away from faith, and God has no need of their belief or any creature; He is praised for His favors.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The rejecters said this to belittle human beings as messengers from God to people like themselves.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مقاتل | reports | God is independent of your deeds.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · علي | reports | God is worthy of praise from His creatures for the blessings He gives them.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Alternatively, God is inherently deserving of their praise.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas gives a third explanation: God loves His servants to praise Him.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Bashar and insan mean the same thing, though their names have different derivations.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Bashar derives from the visible surface of the skin.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Insan may derive from uns, human sociability.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Alternatively, insan may derive from forgetfulness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | They disbelieved in the messengers and turned away from the proof.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مقاتل | reports | God needs no obedience from His servants by virtue of His sovereign power.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Alternatively, God had no need of further proof after making the signs and explanation clear enough to guide people.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p21/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · البراء بن عازب | reports | God is independent of your charitable gifts.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p325/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | They viewed guidance only from the human, created side and fell into confusion; seeing through reality would free them from false multiplicity and changing conditions by witnessing God's decree.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p485#3/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | God has no need of their faith or worship.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:64:5-6/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Their punishment came because messengers brought clear proofs and they rejected them.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:64:5-6/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | They considered it implausible that human beings could guide them; “human” is collective, explaining the plural “guide us.”
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:64:5-6/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | They disbelieved and turned away from faith.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:64:5-6/r5] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God has no need of their faith or of His creatures and is praiseworthy in His actions.
[JISHUMI:v10p6955/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | In bi-annahu, the hāʾ may be an expletive support or a pronoun referring to firmness.
[JISHUMI:v10p6955/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The punishment came because messengers brought clear proofs, arguments, and miracles, but people denied them and turned away; God needs neither them nor their worship and only commands for their benefit.
[JISHUMI:v10p6955/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | God is described as self-sufficient and praiseworthy: either praised, or deserving praise for blessing people despite their disbelief.
[JISHUMI:v10p6956/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The phrase that punishment came because of their deeds shows that punishment is deserved for sins, which are their own acts.
[JISHUMI:v10p6956/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | By asking whether ordinary humans could guide them, the people showed their inability to answer the manifest miracle and shifted to an irrelevant objection; prophethood concerns benefit, not shared species.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p141#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | In ‘human messengers guide us,’ البشر is grammatically singular but collective in meaning, with إنسان as its individual; they object that a human like them guides them.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p141#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | God has no need of their faith and is independent of creation, praiseworthy in His acts.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p318#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Earlier unbelievers' objection resembles Quraysh's rejection of human resurrection and prophethood, compounded by envy of the chosen messenger.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p318#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | أبشر is nominative as the sentence's subject.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p318#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The plural in يهدوننا reflects that بشر names the human species: they ask whether people are to guide them.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p318#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Their destruction became manifest, showing they could not harm God; He was eternally self-sufficient.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p318#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Although استفعل usually indicates seeking or attaining through seeking, this wording fits because God's self-sufficiency became manifest after their destruction.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The nations were destroyed after messengers brought clear proofs and people rejected them as mere humans, out of contempt for following a human messenger and pride in ancestral religion.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They disbelieved in God, denied His messengers, and turned away from accepting them and reflecting on their signs.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God needs no obedience from His servants; He obligated them for their own benefit, not from need for their worship.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · قول آخر | reports | Another explanation is that the proof and clarification God showed them made any further call to guidance unnecessary.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God is independent of people's deeds and worthy of their praise for His blessings; alternatively, He is praised in all His acts because they are wholly beneficent.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | In dhālika bi-annahu, the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter or affair.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Abashar is an indefinite subject licensed by the question; interrogative and negative clauses allow such subjects because they are non-assertive.
[TABRISI:64:6-8/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · قول آخر | reports | Alternatively, abashar is the subject of an omitted verb explained by yahdūnanā; the verb is elided because a verb-first question is more natural.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p281#4/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Their punishment came because their messengers brought clear signs and they denied them, asking whether people like themselves could guide them.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p281#4/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Bashar is a collective noun meaning people, although its grammatical form is singular.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p281#4/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | They disbelieved and turned away, that is, they turned away from faith.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p281#4/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | God had no need of their faith or worship.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p21#2/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “They turned away” is not redundant with “they disbelieved”: their rejection of human messengers expressed complete refusal and turning away, hence both verbs.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p21#2/r14] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكشاف | reports | The Kashshāf explains the sequence as God’s independence becoming manifest when He did not compel them to faith, despite having power to do so.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p21#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “That is because” means the matter was that they objected to a human messenger guiding them; they did not object to worshipping stone idols, so they disbelieved and turned away.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p21#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God had been independent of their obedience and worship from pre-eternit

[QURTUBI-FULL:64:6/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | That punishment is for disbelieving the messengers who came to them.
[QURTUBI-FULL:64:6/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says God's clear proof made Him need no further summons to guide them.
